column13: A wedding at the historic Tersane Istanbul shipyard, where every printed piece was designed as one language. The stationery took its cues from the architecture of the building, so the invitation, the menu, the signage, and the seating all belonged to the same world.
column14: The stationery is where the wedding's concept turned into something a guest could hold. Its language came from the shipyard itself, drawn out in minimal typography, metallic finishes, and exhibition-style layouts. That register held across every surface, from the card in a hand to the menu on the table to the signage on the wall. The whole printed side of the night read as one design, tied back to the larger world built for the day.
column21: A complete stationery system was designed specifically for the event, including invitations, menus, signage, seating elements, printed materials, and custom graphic applications. The visual identity drew from the project’s architectural narrative, combining minimal typography, metallic finishes, and exhibition inspired layouts to create a consistent experience across all physical touchpoints.
column22:
Set inside the historic shipyard at Tersane Istanbul, this wedding was approached as a single design project rather than a series of decorative moments. Virtually Ever After led the creative direction end to end, shaping a world where architecture, graphics, film, and objects all spoke the same language.
The concept came before any palette. Drawing on the industrial past of the shipyard, its monumental scale and its closeness to the sea, a visual identity was built around a digital-romantic sensibility: something close to a metaverse wedding, romantic yet unmistakably digital. A wireframe aesthetic ran through every visual, borrowed from the language of architectural plans and used to strip each idea down to its clearest form.
The full graphic suite was designed in-house. From the save the date and invitation to the menus, seating plan, and signage, every printed touchpoint followed one visual language of minimal typography, metallic finishes, and custom-fabricated metal elements. The invitation was conceived as a piece of video art and delivered as a message rather than a printed card. The dinner menu was drawn as an isometric exploded diagram, built from photographs taken during the tasting.
A series of site-specific moving-image installations was created for the evening and projected across the historic walls. Some were purely diagrammatic animations tracing the textures and arched forms of the venue; others layered the couple's own wireframe portraits and sped-up black-and-white cuts of favourite films, alongside animated reinterpretations of Matisse and Francis Bacon paintings rendered in the same aesthetic. As the night moved into the after-party, the films loosened up, shifting toward overlaid design animations and lighter, more playful internet references. The projections evolved throughout the evening, responding to each moment and becoming part of the rhythm of the night.
The same visual world extended into the wedding film, produced in collaboration with Easthaus. The original pieces created for the day were woven into the documentary footage, blending both into a single layered, mixed-media narrative that captured not only the events of the day but the creative vision behind it.
Across stationery, spatial design, and moving image, the project became a complete environment: a wedding designed the way a studio designs its own launch.

column13: The moving image projected across the shipyard walls through the night. A run of films in the wedding's inverted-monochrome wireframe language, built entirely from the couple's own world: their favourite artworks, the objects on their tables, the shape of the bridal bouquet, and the places their relationship passed through.
column14: Across the evening, the historic walls of Tersane Istanbul became a screen. Every film shared one language, an inverted-monochrome wireframe drawn from architectural plans, and every one came from the couple. Their chosen artworks were remixed into that register. The continuous metal wave that defined the tables was projected beside the DAS Pieces favours until the two objects spoke to each other and the room took on their aura, and the guests watched the design they were sitting inside referenced live. Another film followed the favour's shape as it became the bridal bouquet, then the ceremony decor, then an abstract reading of the ceremony itself. A looping logo film carried the couple from the Virtually Ever After mark they built into a celebration of rabbits and back again. The couple appeared in wireframe over the films, and the thresholds of their relationship were rendered as terrain from satellite data and contour lines. Graphics were laid over four selected films and set against older black-and-white footage, putting the digital next to the romantic and the new next to the old, straight out of the name Virtually Ever After. Four fully edited films played through the night, loosening toward lighter, more playful references as the evening moved into the after-party.

column13: The moving-image library for STATUS CO, built across art direction, motion, and sound. A run of reels that carry the brand from its 3D gallery site to the products, the launch, and the pop-up's most playful pieces.
column14: The reels document the brand's world and turn its products into content. The experimental 3D gallery site was recorded straight off the screen, and a flat gallery floor was moved tectonically until it became the STATUS CO exhibition platform. column13: Edetri is a tableware brand in glass and ceramic that gathers a community around its events. Ahead of a new metal-and-glass line, we studied where the brand's identity could go next and set it into a board the two sides could shape together.
column14: The question was where Edetri could take its identity for a new era. We looked at it on three fronts at once, its graphics, its language, and its attitude, ahead of a collection moving into metal and glass. The findings lived in a board built specifically for the brand. It carried annotation and comment tools, so Edetri and the studio could mark what worked and what did not directly on it, and settle the new direction as one decision.
column21: Presented at Mercado Design Days, Edetri was approached as a full brand strategy project rather than a one-off campaign. Virtually Ever After consolidated the brand's product and event-focused work under a single unified language, reproducing every visual through a new art direction and compiling it into a booklet. The system extended from a digital brand board to printed cardboards handed to visitors during the event, giving Edetri one coherent voice across strategy, print, and web.
column22:
Presented at Mercado Design Days, Edetri was approached as a complete brand strategy project rather than a single campaign or product line. Virtually Ever After led the art direction end to end, building a system where strategy, print, and digital presence all spoke the same language.
The work began by consolidating Edetri's existing output. Product photography, event material, and past projects were gathered and reproduced within a single new art direction, so that a body of work made across different moments could finally read as one brand. This unified language then became the foundation for everything that followed.
At the center of the project was a booklet that compiled these reinterpreted projects into one curated document, part portfolio, part manifesto for the brand's new era. From the booklet, a set of cardboards was designed and produced to be shared with visitors during Mercado Design Days, translating the printed language into a tactile object people could carry away from the event.
Alongside the print work, a digital touchpoint was developed: a brand strategy board built as part of a cohesive identity and web system, extending the same visual thinking into an online presence.
Across strategy, print, and web, the project gave Edetri a single unified identity, a new era approach where every touchpoint, physical or digital, belonged to the same world.

column44:
For SGM, Virtually Ever After produced a complete urban-scale site analysis for a hotel project located in Gazipaşa, Alanya, on Turkey's southern coast.

Delivered as a full print document, the analysis functions as the groundwork for everything that follows, establishing a shared, evidence-based understanding of the location before architectural design begins.

column13: Selin Gencoglu paints demons in dark, unsettling rooms, work that runs on chaos, fear, and tension. Her website was built as the place those paintings come from, a 3D world rendered as their source.
column14: The site treats the paintings as if they all came out of one world, so we built that world in 3D and made it the source of the imagery. A figure was pulled from each canvas, sketched again by Selin's own hand, and placed inside an environment built from scratch. Visitors step into that atmosphere and move through it themselves, becoming part of the experience the paintings describe. The website holds her work the way the paintings hold their rooms.

The result is a spatial online presence that treats the artist's work as something to move through rather than simply view.
column22:
For Istanbul-based painter Selin Gencoglu, Virtually Ever After designed an interactive website shaped entirely around her visual identity and artistic practice, a digital presence built to hold the work the way a space might, rather than a conventional portfolio.
The site was conceived as an immersive environment. Instead of presenting the paintings as a flat grid, the design treats the artist's world as something to move through, letting her imagery set the pace and atmosphere of the experience.
To open the site, one of the artist's signature paintings was taken as source material, uncropped, and animated. What is normally seen as a fixed, framed image was extended and set into slow motion, becoming a moving portal into the rest of the practice. This piece establishes the tone before a single work is browsed.
Across web design and moving image, the project gave the artist a cohesive digital presence, an online space that feels closer to an artwork in its own right than to a standard website.

column22:
For New York-based dating app Laila, Virtually Ever After developed both a landing page and a cinematic short, built around a single idea: the brand's "action-first" philosophy and its rejection of passive, endless scrolling in favour of real-world connection.
The landing page was designed as a cinematic, fluid interface rather than a static product page. Its rhythm borrows from the restless pulse of New York, moving with the same energy the app is trying to encourage in its users, and framing Laila less as software and more as an invitation to step outside and meet.
That philosophy was then translated into film. The short is a high-energy visual narrative that turns "action-first" into motion, a fast, kinetic piece that prioritizes real-world encounters over the interface itself, carrying the pace and texture of the city into every cut.
Across web and film, the project gave Laila a coherent visual language: cinematic, kinetic, and unmistakably tied to the energy of NYC.

column13: The DROP 001 pop-up at ArtShow Galeriler Buluşması 2026, built end to end through a digital process. Over a hundred objects were modelled at 1:1 before anything was made, turning an empty file into a three-day experience.
column14: The pop-up ran entirely through digital process, with the client inside every step. column13: Architectural films for the Luxembourg office Novantatre. Their buildings turned into things you watch: a year gathered into a pop-up book, a residence told as a small story, and an early render that reads a house before it is resolved.
column14: The first was a yearbook. At the close of the year, the buildings finished over twelve months were gathered into a cut-out book built from borderless cardboard in the brand's Ancora bordeaux. It opens onto five projects, and each page lifts into a model that the camera walks into. A residential reel took a different route, with urgency as its key word. It sets a small story inside the building, someone moving through empty rooms with the sense of being followed and finally getting out, so a twist of narrative carries the project and turns the architecture into the subject of something happening. A third piece, rendered straight out of Blender from a rough draft file, gave the client a fast read on the spatial quality of a house before any detail was resolved.

The work opened with a brand strategy launch film that introduced Novantatre's language to the world, less a promotional clip than a considered piece of motion that framed the office's design thinking as a coherent identity from the outset.
From there, the focus moved to the work itself. A series of architectural reels was produced around the studio's Luxembourg residential project, structured as a sequential, archive-like narrative that guides the viewer through spatial layers and material detail. Draft renders were developed into the same filmic language, so that even in-progress material read as part of a single, deliberate story rather than isolated visualization.
Across direction and film, the project gave Novantatre a cinematic, platform-ready presence, architecture presented not as static images but as an unfolding spatial narrative.

column13: A showcase film for the DAS Pieces lamp collection, built like an old pull-tab children's book. Each pull turns a page and brings the next product into view.
column14: The film gives the collection a rhythm borrowed from a pull-tab picture book. Each pull brings the next page, and a DAS Pieces product arrives in its own photograph, one after another. The device lets each piece land on its own before the next is drawn in, giving the lamps a small sense of play while keeping every product clearly its own.

For Istanbul-based industrial design brand DAS Pieces, Virtually Ever After led creative direction and video production around the studio's lamp collection.
Rather than presenting the pieces as a conventional product catalogue, the showcase film reinterpreted each lamp through a digital narrative, situating every object within its own atmosphere and light. The approach treated the collection less as a set of products to document and more as a series of designed environments, letting each piece establish its own mood.
The result is a product film that carries the brand's industrial-design sensibility into a cinematic, atmospheric register, turning a lamp collection into a considered visual story.

column9: Immersive Web Design, Art Direction, Booklet Design
column13: C2W2's runway and avatar collection left a large archive behind. We organised all of it inside an interface everyone already knows, a desktop, and paired it with a viewer that turns each avatar in full motion.
column14: The finder holds the whole archive inside a desktop file system. Folders open, files are clicked through, and the collection is explored the way people sort their own machines every day. Browsing a website usually feels like visiting one, so C2W2 was built to feel like the desktop underneath it, the place that feels like home when you minimise the window. Alongside it sits the selector, a viewer for the 48 avatars drawn in a Blade Runner register. Each design turns in full 360 motion with its data beside it, so a garment can be read and studied in the same moment it is seen.
column21: C2W2 is a virtual runway project brought together by Virtually Ever After across web and print. An immersive website maps the full virtual fashion experience into a single curated layout, an avatars interface extends it into an interactive hybrid space, and a booklet bridges the digital visualization with tactile literature, designed as an art object in its own right.
column22:
C2W2 is a virtual runway project for which Virtually Ever After led immersive web design, art direction, and booklet design, building a single visual system that spans digital and print.
At its center is a website that maps the entire virtual fashion experience into one curated graphical layout. Rather than scattering the project across pages, the design consolidates the runway, its concepts, and its imagery into a single navigable environment. An avatars interface extends this into a more interactive, hybrid space, letting the project's digital fashion figures be explored directly.
Alongside the web work, a booklet was designed to bridge digital visualization with tactile literature. Conceived as an art object rather than a simple catalogue, it gives the virtual project a physical, collectible counterpart, something to hold as well as browse.
Across web and print, C2W2 became a complete world for virtual fashion, curated so that its digital and physical forms belong to the same language.

column13: A website for the Milan digital design studio Decentralize Design, holding their entire output inside a single frame. It was structured architecturally, so you move through the work the way you move through a building.
column14: We built the site together with the studio, holding all of their output inside one UI frame and delivering it piece by piece. The structure was approached architecturally, its sections flowing into one another in a clear hierarchy. The result reads like a building you travel floor by floor, giving a digital studio a home that carries its own spatial logic.
column21: For Milan-based design studio Decentralize Design, Virtually Ever After built a full digital identity spanning web, film, and brand strategy. Two interactive websites, one for the studio's spatial practice, one for the artist behind it, share a signature clockwork visual language, while a two-minute cinematic short deconstructs the studio's virtual world-building process through precise motion graphics and spatial documentation.
column22:
For Milan-based design studio Decentralize Design, Virtually Ever After developed a complete digital identity across web, film, and brand strategy, a system built for a digital-first, spatial creative practice.
The work spans two connected websites. One presents Decentralize Design as a studio, showcasing its spatial expertise through a signature clockwork visual identity; the other is a digital presence for decentralize*, the Milan-based artist behind the practice, built as a spatial and graphical world in its own right. Together they let the studio and the individual voice behind it share one coherent language.
This identity was then set into motion through a two-minute cinematic short. The film deconstructs the studio's virtual world-building process, using precise motion graphics and spatial documentation to show not just the finished work but the way it is made.
Across web, film, and strategy, the project gave Decentralize Design a spatial, digital-first presence, an identity that treats world-building itself as the studio's signature.

column13: decentralize* works across several mediums, and the archive it left behind carries disorder and structure in equal measure. The site rebuilds that same condition digitally.
column14: Years of work in different formats were mapped and organised into a single navigable environment. The site holds the mess and the system at once, letting the range of the practice stay legible without being tidied away. The outcome matches how decentralize* actually works: many mediums, one place that carries them all.
